title: Russian Doll Envelopes
notes:
Task: Nest the maximum number of envelopes with both dimensions strictly increasing.
Idea: Sort widths ascending and equal-width heights descending, then compute a strictly increasing subsequence of heights.
Invariant: tails[length-1] is the smallest ending height found for a subsequence of that length.
Edge cases: Descending equal-width heights prevent two envelopes of the same width from entering one increasing subsequence.
complexity_reason: Sorting and binary-searching each height dominate the runtime.

title: Russian Doll Envelopes
notes:
Task: Find the longest chain of envelopes with strictly increasing widths and heights.
Idea: Sort by width ascending and height descending for ties, then run the LIS tails algorithm on heights.
Invariant: tails stores the smallest possible final height for each increasing-chain length.
Edge cases: Equal widths are sorted by descending height so they cannot form a valid chain together.
complexity_reason: The envelope sort and per-envelope binary search are O(n log n).

title: Count Numbers with Unique Digits
notes:
Task: Count numbers in [0,10^n) whose decimal digits are all distinct.
Idea: Count one-digit values, then count longer numbers by choosing a nonzero first digit and unused digits afterward.
Invariant: unique counts the number of valid numbers of the current digit length.
Edge cases: n=0 counts only zero; no number can have more than ten distinct decimal digits.
complexity_reason: The loop runs at most nine times and uses constant storage.

title: Count Numbers with Unique Digits
notes:
Task: Count nonnegative integers below 10^n that have no repeated decimal digit.
Idea: Add the count for each digit length using 9 choices for the first digit and decreasing choices for subsequent digits.
Invariant: unique is the count for the current length; total accumulates all shorter lengths.
Edge cases: n=0 returns one for zero, and the number of distinct decimal digits caps the useful length at ten.
complexity_reason: At most nine constant-work iterations are performed.

title: Largest Divisible Subset
notes:
Task: Return a largest subset where every pair is divisible in one direction.
Idea: Sort values and let dp[i] be the largest divisible subset ending at nums[i], storing the previous index.
Invariant: Every predecessor j<i with nums[i] divisible by nums[j] can extend the best subset ending at j.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty subset; sorting ensures divisibility chains can be built in increasing order.
complexity_reason: The nested pair scan compares each earlier value for every current value.

title: Largest Divisible Subset
notes:
Task: Find a maximum-size subset whose values form a divisibility chain.
Idea: Sort the array and use quadratic DP to record the best chain ending at each value.
Invariant: dp[i] is the longest chain ending at nums[i], and prev[i] links to its predecessor.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty list; all values are assumed positive as in the problem constraints.
complexity_reason: The nested loop performs O(n^2) divisibility checks and stores DP/predecessor arrays.

title: Wiggle Subsequence
notes:
Task: Find the longest subsequence whose adjacent differences alternate strictly positive and negative.
Idea: Maintain the best lengths ending with an upward step and a downward step.
Invariant: up is best after an increase; down is best after a decrease.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; equal adjacent values change neither state.
complexity_reason: The algorithm compares adjacent values once and stores two lengths.

title: Wiggle Subsequence
notes:
Task: Return the length of the longest subsequence with alternating strict rises and falls.
Idea: Track the best subsequence length ending in an up-step and a down-step.
Invariant: Each state can extend only the opposite-direction state when the next adjacent pair changes direction.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; equal adjacent values are ignored.
complexity_reason: One scan updates two integer states.

title: Combination Sum IV
notes:
Task: Count ordered sequences of supplied positive numbers that sum to target.
Idea: For each total, add the number of sequences that reach the total after choosing each possible final number.
Invariant: dp[t] counts ordered sequences summing to t using the available values.
Edge cases: dp[0]=1 represents the empty prefix; positive numbers ensure dependencies point to smaller totals.
complexity_reason: Each total checks all n candidate numbers and stores target+1 states.

title: Combination Sum IV
notes:
Task: Count ordered sequences that add up to target.
Idea: Build dp[t] by summing dp[t-x] for every number x that can be the last element.
Invariant: All smaller totals are computed before the current total, so each transition uses completed states.
Edge cases: dp[0] is one for the empty sequence; all nums values are positive.
complexity_reason: The nested loops perform at most target times n transitions.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
notes:
Task: Find the kth smallest value in a matrix sorted by rows and columns.
Idea: Binary-search the value interval and count entries no greater than each midpoint using a staircase walk.
Invariant: If at least k values are <= mid, the answer is at most mid; otherwise it is larger.
Edge cases: The matrix is nonempty and k is valid; duplicate values are counted individually.
complexity_reason: Each value-search iteration counts in O(n) using a staircase scan.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
notes:
Task: Return the kth smallest matrix entry, counting duplicates as separate entries.
Idea: Binary-search the possible value and count entries <= mid from the bottom-left corner.
Invariant: The count test narrows the answer to the smallest value whose count is at least k.
Edge cases: A valid nonempty square matrix is assumed; the scan moves only upward or rightward.
complexity_reason: Each binary-search step performs an O(n) staircase count.

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
notes:
Task: Support insert, remove, and random retrieval in average constant time.
Idea: Store values densely in a list and map each value to its current index.
Invariant: Every map entry points to the matching value in the list; removal swaps the last value into the removed slot.
Edge cases: Insert returns false for existing values; removing a missing value returns false.
complexity_reason: List indexing, hash-map updates, and random index selection are expected constant time.

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
notes:
Task: Implement insert, remove, and uniform random selection with average O(1) operations.
Idea: Keep a dense list and map values to indices; remove by swapping the final value into the removed slot.
Invariant: The map always identifies each stored value's current list position.
Edge cases: Existing inserts and absent removals return false; getRandom assumes the collection is nonempty.
complexity_reason: ArrayList access and HashMap operations are expected constant time.

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed
notes:
Task: Support average O(1) insertion, removal of one occurrence, and random retrieval with duplicates.
Idea: Store every occurrence in a list and track its indices in a set for each value.
Invariant: Each stored index appears in the corresponding value's index set.
Edge cases: Insert returns true only when the value was previously absent; removal deletes one occurrence, not all copies.
complexity_reason: Index sets and list operations are expected constant time per occurrence.

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed
notes:
Task: Design a randomized collection that allows duplicates and removes one occurrence at a time.
Idea: Maintain a list of occurrences and a set of indices for each value, swapping the last occurrence into a removed position.
Invariant: Every index set points to exactly the positions occupied by its value.
Edge cases: Insert reports whether the value was absent before insertion; removing a value with no indices returns false.
complexity_reason: The list and hash-based index sets support constant-time average updates.

title: Ransom Note
notes:
Task: Determine whether magazine letters can form ransomNote without reuse.
Idea: Count available magazine characters and consume one count for every ransom-note character.
Invariant: Counts represent the unused supply of each character.
Edge cases: A missing or exhausted character immediately makes construction impossible; empty note is constructible.
complexity_reason: Both strings are scanned and the counter stores at most u distinct characters.

title: Ransom Note
notes:
Task: Check whether the ransom note can be assembled from magazine characters, each used at most once.
Idea: Count magazine letters in a fixed 26-element array and decrement the required letter counts.
Invariant: counts[c] is the remaining supply of lowercase letter c.
Edge cases: A count below zero means the note needs more copies than the magazine contains.
complexity_reason: Each string is scanned once and the fixed alphabet counter uses constant space.

title: Lexicographical Numbers
notes:
Task: List integers 1 through n in lexicographical order.
Idea: Walk the decimal-prefix tree by descending to curr*10 when possible, otherwise backtracking and incrementing the last digit.
Invariant: curr is the next integer in lexical preorder after the prior output.
Edge cases: The traversal backs out of trailing nines and prefixes beyond n; n is positive.
complexity_reason: Each integer is emitted once with amortized constant traversal work.

title: Lexicographical Numbers
notes:
Task: Return the numbers from 1 to n in dictionary order.
Idea: Descend to a ten-times larger prefix if possible; otherwise move to the next sibling and backtrack past nines.
Invariant: The current number follows preorder traversal of the implicit decimal prefix tree.
Edge cases: Backtracking prevents moving beyond n and handles prefixes ending in repeated nines.
complexity_reason: The traversal emits each value once and uses only a current integer besides the output list.
